firstDiff: Interpreting students' ideas across talk, writing, and images raises a methodological question about which records to preserve. Research on plurilingual identity texts has examined conversations alongside students' written and visual work (Prasad, 2015). A relational account of multiliteracies considers how meaning develops within social and cultural relationships (Simon, 2011). The literacy settings differ from those of secondary science. The same attention to conversations and classroom relationships may help me interpret written and visual work in science.

-

Language proficiency scores offer one account of university students' experiences. A longitudinal study examined academic acculturation alongside English proficiency and achievement, attending to factors a language test score might leave unexplained (Neumann et al., 2023). Conversations with students present a different interpretive challenge. In a Canadian university English-language programme, tensions around racism emerged during a post-semester interview and a private conversation about a student's poem, both examined in a study of a spoken-word-poetry curriculum (Burton, 2024). Both studies concern university language learning. In secondary science, they lead me to consider how the setting and relationships surrounding a contribution affect what an observer can reasonably conclude from it.
